The cosmological argument reasons from the mere existence of a contingent, dependent universe, one that could evidently have failed to exist at all, or that might well have existed in some quite different form than it actually and in fact does, to the necessary existence of some further, non-contingent and necessary being capable of adequately explaining that contingent universe's own existence, since an endless, infinite regress of merely contingent causes is held by proponents of the argument never genuinely and finally to explain why there is a universe at all rather than, quite possibly, simply nothing whatsoever. Critics have long objected that the argument illegitimately assumes every contingent thing must have some further, external explanatory cause, an assumption that is itself far from self-evident, and further that even granting a necessary being's existence for the sake of argument, nothing in the argument's own strict logical structure actually and specifically establishes that this necessary being must additionally possess the traditional further theistic attributes of personal agency, benevolence, or active providential care for the created world.

The teleological, or design, argument instead reasons from the observed order, evident complexity and apparent purposiveness found within the natural world, comparable in these specific respects to the evident, easily recognisable design apparent in human artefacts, to the existence of an intelligent designer as the most adequate explanation for such observed order and complexity. David Hume's classical and carefully developed critique challenges the argument's own crucial underlying analogy directly, noting that the universe as a whole differs quite considerably from any of the comparatively small-scale human artefacts on which the analogy actually depends and from which it is originally drawn, and further and more radically suggesting that even granting some form of designer for the sake of argument, evolutionary or other purely naturalistic processes might in principle equally well and equally adequately account for the same observed appearance of order and complexity in the natural world, without any need to invoke a further, additional designing intelligence at all.

The ontological argument attempts a distinctively different and more purely rationalist strategy again, reasoning entirely from the mere concept or definition of God alone, typically as a being than which no greater can be conceived, directly to that same being's own actual, necessary existence, on the specific ground that a being that genuinely existed in reality, and not merely as a concept confined to the mind alone, would thereby be, simply in virtue of its actual existence, still greater than a merely conceived, non-existent being sharing all the very same other attributes. Kant's well-known and influential objection holds that existence is not, properly and carefully considered, a real, substantive predicate or property at all, comparable to other genuine substantive properties such as being wise or being powerful, but is instead merely the logical positing of a subject as actually existing in reality, so that no amount of purely conceptual analysis of a mere concept, however initially impressive, rich or exalted that concept may otherwise be, can validly and legitimately establish that any object whatsoever corresponding to that concept in fact and in reality actually exists. Taken together, these three classical arguments and their correspondingly serious, carefully developed objections illustrate the genuine and continuing difficulty of establishing God's existence through unaided reason alone, without recourse to prior religious faith, revelation or an antecedently accepted scriptural authority.

content_items.title: The Problem of Evil and the Major Theodicies
content_items.body:
The problem of evil poses what many philosophers of religion regard as the single most serious and enduring challenge to traditional theistic belief, since it appears to expose a direct and troubling tension between three claims that classical theism typically wishes, and generally needs, to affirm simultaneously: that God is entirely omnipotent, that God is entirely omniscient, and that God is entirely and perfectly good, together with the further, seemingly obvious and undeniable empirical observation that the actual world nonetheless clearly and evidently contains a very great deal of genuine, serious and often seemingly quite gratuitous suffering and evil. The logical version of the problem argues that these several claims are, strictly and simply taken together, flatly and outright logically inconsistent with one another, since a being that were genuinely all-powerful could straightforwardly prevent any and all evil altogether, a being that were genuinely all-knowing would certainly and necessarily know of any and all evil in advance of its occurrence, and a being that were genuinely and perfectly good would surely and necessarily want to prevent such evil from occurring at all, given both the knowledge and the requisite power to do so. The rather more modest and more widely and generally accepted evidential version of the problem instead argues only, and more cautiously, that the sheer scale, apparent gratuitousness and often deeply troubling and seemingly pointless distribution of suffering actually observed within the real world, considered honestly and directly, constitutes very strong evidence against, even if it does not amount to a strictly and formally decisive logical disproof of, the existence of such a being.

Theodicies are the various sustained philosophical and theological attempts to reconcile evil's plain, evident and undeniable existence with belief in such a being, and two theodicies in particular have proven especially influential and widely discussed within this ongoing debate. The free-will defence, most notably and influentially associated with the philosopher Alvin Plantinga, though it has significant historical antecedents extending back to Augustine and other earlier thinkers, argues that a great deal of the actual evil we observe in the world, specifically so-called moral evil, evil brought about directly through the freely chosen and voluntary actions of other genuinely free created agents, is best understood as a necessary and unavoidable cost of God's having freely and deliberately chosen to create genuinely free, rather than merely and entirely pre-programmed, deterministic, agents, since authentic and meaningful moral freedom logically and necessarily requires the very real, live and ever-present possibility of these same free agents sometimes choosing wrongly and evilly rather than rightly and well, and a world genuinely containing free creatures capable of real moral good is held, on balance, to be a distinctly and significantly better world overall than one containing only fully determined, pre-programmed beings incapable of ever really choosing or doing evil at all, even though such fully determined beings would, for that very same reason, also be equally incapable of ever really choosing or doing any genuine, freely willed moral good either.

The soul-making theodicy, most notably and carefully associated with the philosopher John Hick, offers instead a rather different, and in certain key respects considerably broader, explanatory strategy, arguing that at least a great deal of the evil and suffering we actually observe and encounter within the world, including a considerable measure of so-called natural evil, suffering directly and specifically arising from natural causes and processes such as disease, earthquakes or other similar natural disasters, rather than from other agents' free moral choices, serves an essential, indispensable and ultimately positive developmental and formative purpose within a divinely intended and carefully designed process of gradual soul-making, a difficult, at times painful, but ultimately valuable process through which human beings are enabled to develop, over time and often specifically and only through direct, concrete and lived confrontation with genuine difficulty, hardship and adversity, such genuinely valuable moral and spiritual qualities as courage, resilience, compassion and real, hard-won and ultimately meaningful spiritual growth and maturity, virtues and qualities that, Hick argues, simply and straightforwardly could not otherwise plausibly develop, be exercised, or be genuinely and meaningfully cultivated at all within a comparatively effortless, entirely comfortable, and altogether frictionless world lacking any real difficulty, resistance or genuine adversity whatsoever. Assessing the ultimate adequacy of either of these two theodicies, or of the several others also commonly proposed and discussed, requires weighing carefully and honestly whether the specific, positive explanatory good each theodicy actually and specifically identifies in turn genuinely and adequately justifies, or is instead simply and straightforwardly outweighed by, the sheer observed and undeniable scale, severity, apparent randomness and often seemingly quite excessive and gratuitous distribution of the suffering that we do, as a matter of simple and evident empirical fact, actually observe all around us within the real world as it actually and concretely is.
